ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A simplified device for detecting the energy of particles in a gravitational field within a vacuum environment is shown in the figure. $P$ is a particle source that continuously emits particles with the same mass but different initial velocities horizontally to the right. A detection screen $AB$ with a height of $h$ is placed vertically, at a horizontal distance of $L$ from point $P$. The upper end $A$ of the screen is also at a height difference of $h$ from point $P$, and the gravitational acceleration is $g$.

1. If the particle hits the midpoint of the detection screen $AB$, find the time of flight of the particle in the air.
2. The range of initial velocities of particles that can be detected by the screen
3. If the magnitudes of the velocities of the particles hitting points $A$ and $B$ on the detection screen are equal, find the relationship between $L$ and $h$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, the particle source P is located at the upper left, and the particle is emitted horizontally to the right from P, with the initial velocity labeled v. Below P there is a vertical dashed line as a height reference. On the right side there is a vertical detection screen AB, with A at the upper end and B at the lower end; the horizontal distance from the detection screen to the vertical line where P is located is labeled L. In the figure, the height of A is h lower than P, and B is again h lower than A, so relative to P, the vertical falling distance of A is h, the vertical falling distance of B is 2h, and the falling distance of the midpoint of screen AB is 3h/2. Reasoning: Take P as the coordinate origin, horizontally to the right as the positive x direction, and vertically downward as the positive y direction. The particle is projected horizontally, therefore x=vt, y=(1/2)gt^2. 1. If the particle hits the midpoint of AB, the vertical falling distance of the midpoint relative to P is s=(h+2h)/2=3h/2. From (1/2)gt^2=3h/2, obtain gt^2=3h, so t=sqrt(3h/g). 2. When the particle can be detected by the screen, the vertical falling distance when reaching x=L must be between h and 2h. Since t=L/v, s=(1/2)g(L/v)^2=gL^2/(2v^2). It is required that h <= gL^2/(2v^2) <= 2h. Solve the inequality for positive v: from gL^2/(2v^2) >= h obtain v <= L sqrt(g/(2h)); from gL^2/(2v^2) <= 2h obtain v >= L sqrt(g/(4h)). Therefore the speed range is L sqrt(g/(4h)) <= v <= L sqrt(g/(2h)). 3. When hitting A, the fall is h, so (1/2)g t_A^2=h, t_A=sqrt(2h/g), and the corresponding horizontal initial velocity v_A=L/t_A=L sqrt(g/(2h)). When hitting B, the fall is 2h, so (1/2)g t_B^2=2h, t_B=sqrt(4h/g), and the corresponding horizontal initial velocity v_B=L/t_B=L sqrt(g/(4h)). The square of the velocity when striking A is v_A^2+(gt_A)^2=gL^2/(2h)+2gh. The square of the velocity when striking B is v_B^2+(gt_B)^2=gL^2/(4h)+4gh. If the magnitudes of the two are equal, then gL^2/(2h)+2gh=gL^2/(4h)+4gh. Simplifying gives L^2/(4h)=2h, that is L^2=8h^2. Since L>0, L=2sqrt(2)h.
